The words

When I survey the wondrous cross
On which the Prince of glory died,
My richest gain I count but loss,
And pour contempt on all my pride.

Forbid it, Lord, that I should boast,
Save in the death of Christ my God:
All the vain things that charm me most,
I sacrifice them to His blood.

See from His head, His hands, His feet,
Sorrow and love flow mingled down:
Did e’er such love and sorrow meet,
Or thorns compose so rich a crown?

Were the whole realm of nature mine,
That were a present far too small;
Love so amazing, so divine,
Demands my soul, my life, my all.

How to sing it from the solfa

  • Find doh first. Play or hum D and sing d r m f s up from it, so the whole choir has the key in their ears before you start.
  • Pitch the first note. The tune starts on d (D), on the word “When”, as a pickup before the first full bar.
  • Count the time. 3/4 means three crotchet beats in each bar. In the grid every cell is half a crotchet: a dash (–) holds the note before it, and _ is a rest.
  • Know the notes. The tune uses d r m f s l t and the chromatic fe. A comma after a note (s,) is the octave below; an apostrophe (d') is the octave above.

About the hymn

Isaac Watts published this hymn in Hymns and Spiritual Songs (1707), as a meditation on Galatians 6:14. Edward Miller adapted the tune ROCKINGHAM in 1790 from an older melody; in America the words are also sung to Lowell Mason's HAMBURG.

  • Words (1707): Isaac Watts (1674–1748)
  • Adapted the melody (1790): Edward Miller (1735–1807)

Tune ROCKINGHAM by Edward Miller (1735–1807); words by Isaac Watts (1674–1748).

Questions about When I Survey the Wondrous Cross

What is the doh of When I Survey the Wondrous Cross?

In this version, in D major, doh is D. If your choir sings it in another key, doh moves to the new key note and every solfa syllable stays the same — that is what movable doh means.

What note does When I Survey the Wondrous Cross start on?

It starts on d (D in D major), a pickup on the word “When” before the first full bar. Find doh first, then sing up or down to d.

Is When I Survey the Wondrous Cross in the public domain?

Yes. Isaac Watts died in 1748, Edward Miller died in 1807; the words were first published in 1707 and the music in 1790. Everyone named died before 1955 and both were published before 1929, so the hymn is out of copyright in the UK, the EU, the United States and Nigeria. Modern arrangements and translations can still be under copyright.
